questions.q: On a Plan 5 student loan you earn {s} a year. How much do you repay in a year?
A graduate with a Plan 5 loan earns £22,000 a year. How much do they repay?
options: It depends how much they borrowed
questions.why: Repayments are 9% of income above £25,000, so below the threshold they repay nothing.

questions.q: On Plan 5, borrowing more for university always means paying more each month after you graduate.
questions.why: The monthly repayment depends only on income above the threshold, not on the balance.

questions.q: What happens to a Plan 5 balance that hasn't been repaid after 40 years?
options: It moves to a credit card
You must pay it all at once
questions.why: Plan 5 loans are written off 40 years after you're first due to repay. Plan 2 loans after 30.

questions.q: An apprentice on the minimum apprentice rate of £8.00 an hour works {h} hours a week. What's their gross weekly pay?
questions.why: {h} × £8.00 = {answer} a week. Many employers pay apprentices more than the minimum.

questions.q: In England, what's the maximum tenancy deposit a landlord can usually take (rent under £50,000 a year)?
questions.why: Five weeks' rent, protected in a government-approved scheme. Holding deposits are capped at one week.

questions.q: Match each situation to how council tax usually works.
pairs: Full-time students only in the home
Full bill, split however they agree
The bill is the household's, not yours
questions.why: Council tax is per home. Discounts and exemptions depend on who lives there.

questions.q: For a typical renter, put these costs in order from biggest to smallest.
questions.why: Rent dominates most budgets. Council tax and energy are usually next, then smaller bills.

questions.q: What is the interest rate on a Plan 5 student loan set to?
questions.why: Plan 5 interest is RPI inflation (4.1% from September 2026), so the balance doesn't grow above inflation.

questions.q: Explain why people often say a Plan 5 student loan works more like a tax than a normal debt.

ideas.label: You repay a share (9%) of income above a threshold, not a fixed amount based on what you owe
Anything left after 40 years is written off, so lower earners don't repay it all

questions.model: You repay 9% of what you earn above £25,000, through payroll like tax, so the amount depends on your income, not your balance. Whatever's left after 40 years is written off, so people who earn less repay less.
questions.why: Income-linked repayments plus a write-off make it behave like a graduate tax.

tests.answer: You pay 9% of income over the threshold, like tax, and the rest is written off after 40 years.
It depends on how much you earn.
Because the government gives it to you.

questions.q: Explain two things you should compare, beyond first-year pay, when choosing between an apprenticeship and university.

ideas.label: Long-term pay in the specific career (after several years)
Costs: fees, debt, living costs or lost earnings while studying

questions.model: Compare likely pay after several years in the specific career, the total costs (fees, debt, living costs and lost earnings while studying), and whether the career needs a degree, as well as which route you'd enjoy and stick with.
questions.why: Year-one pay is only the start of the story.

tests.answer: Long-term pay in that career, and the cost of debt and living costs at uni, plus whether the job needs a degree.
